items.abstract: <jats:p>Multimodal medical image fusion (MMIF) is an active research topic in computer vision and plays a significant role in clinical medicine. MMIF image quality assessment algorithms serve to evaluate and optimize fusion algorithms. However, current research is still weak in the following two areas, hindering the development of MMIF algorithms in many aspects. First, there are few MMIF image databases to develop quality assessment algorithms. Second, little work has been designed to evaluate the effectiveness of MMIF algorithms and the quality of MMIF images.</jats:p>

items.abstract: An intuitive and comparative approach for melody feature extraction and similarity modeling is introduced in this research, which emphasizes the relationship between the temporal-style feature engineering and various machine learning architectures. Instead of putting forward a solitary predictive model, this research considers the influence of the explicitly engineered temporal features such as deltas, ratios, and rolling statistics on the ability of recurrent, ensemble, and the attention-based models to capture the musical structure. For this purpose, Deep GRU, XGBoost, and a GPT-style Transformer Decoder are assessed on the same spectral and embedding-based feature representations. According to the results, the Deep GRU is the best predictor of all the models being tested ranked by its capability (R² = 0.932) which denotes that not only can the model interpret fast changes in melodies but also see the longer evenness of different motifs in the same piece. XGBoost comes in second (R² = 0.901), providing not only outstanding precision but also easy interpretation via SHAP-based approach, whereas the Transformer Decoder is the weakest, showing the difficulties of attention-centric architectures dealing with engineered features in moderate data conditions through its performance nevertheless (R² = 0.868). Contrary to traditional methods of melody analysis that mainly depend on the building blocks of a system to draw conclusions about the time aspect, this research goes explicitly to the feature level to incorporate the time dynamics, considering them as a representation that is not specific to any model. This approach not only allows for a just, understandable, and less data-consuming comparison between model types but also provides a basis for the practical use of music recommendation, similarity search, and analytics, thereby offering methodological insight to the field of music information retrieval research.

items.abstract: The occurrence of earthquakes at depths greater than 60 km is an enigma in earthquake science, as rocks at greater depths are anticipated to be ductile. Over the past decades, seismologists have reported a variety of rupture characteristics that are distinguishable among shallow (0–60 km), intermediate-depth (60–300 km) and deep-focus (300–700 km) earthquakes. However, their underlying physical mechanisms remain enigmatic. Using machine learning, we show that the previously observed differences in earthquake moment release processes are caused by the Earth’s depth-dependent elastic properties. Despite the presentation of medium rigidity, earthquakes with different generation mechanisms unanimously have similar moment release processes. Our results support a constant strain drop hypothesis, that is, the ratio of coseismic slip to the characteristic rupture length remains largely unchanged for earthquakes at all depths and mechanisms. This finding contests the conventional stress drop hypothesis, leading to a revised definition of earthquake self-similarity. In particular, the moment release invariant property predicts distinct depth- and rigidity-dependencies of critical earthquake parameters, such as rupture duration, geometric scale, and stress drop. These results have broad implications for understanding earthquake physics and assessing seismic hazards.

Methods Step-by-step description of machine learning classification. 1. Model input. We extract 15 STF features for each earthquake in the SCARDEC database. Each earthquake corresponds to a depth category, i.e., shallow or deep earthquakes, and intermediate-depth or deep-focus earthquakes. 2. Training-test split and bootstrapping. As earthquakes at different depths have different populations, to avoid bias in machine learning, we keep the same number of earthquakes from each class for training and testing by bootstrapping. Specifically, in each run of training and testing for shallow-deep classification, we randomly select 932 shallow earthquakes to match the number of deep earthquakes. The training and test data are 1:1. This process is repeated 100 times, and the mean accuracy and standard deviation are calculated. The same procedure is applied to intermediate-depth and deep-focus earthquake classification. 3. Model hyperparameter determination. We use the mean accuracy of the 100 classification results to grid search over tree depth and forest size of the random forest classifiers. The searched optimal tree depth is 8, and the searched optimal forest size is 90 for shallow and deep earthquake classification. The searched optimal tree depth is 4, and the searched optimal forest size is 100 for intermediate-depth and deep-focus earthquake classification. 4. Model performance evaluation. The classification performance is evaluated on the test data set. Each feature is evaluated by Gini importance. Calculation of STF features. The STF features used for classification input include statistical and physical features inherited from previous work (Extended Data Table 1). Duration: The STF duration is calculated by the average cut-off time of 99.9% total moment and 99.9% relative radiated energy (square of STF derivatives). Zero-crossings: zero-crossings measure rupture complexity following Houston21. We filter out the energy above 1 Hz of the STF, transform displacement to velocity by taking the time derivative, and count the zero-crossing numbers of the velocity function. Variance: Variance reflects the overall moment release rate. After removing the effects of M0, a large variance indicates a fast rupture process.

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Surface-related multiple elimination (SRME) has proven to be a robust surface multiple and primary estimation tool for decades. However, surface-related multiple leakage is still commonly observed in SRME-processed results due to imperfect multiple predictions. Usually, adaptive subtraction cannot fully correct for these effects without primary damage. Local primary-and-multiple orthogonalization (LPMO) has recently been proposed to partially mitigate surface multiple leakage, by multiplication of the estimated primaries with a weight function that scales down residual multiples while preserving primaries. The weight function is determined by shaping regularization followed by thresholding and median filtering. Although effective leakage extraction can be achieved, LPMO has a large computational cost due to many conjugate-gradient iterations within the shaping regularization-based inversion framework. Using information on the typical local coherency length of primaries and multiples, a spatially constrained scaled point-by-point division can be used to avoid the iterative inversion within the LPMO method. Based on this, we have adopted a fast LPMO (FLPMO) for surface-related multiple leakage estimation and extraction. Applications on two different field data sets demonstrate the very similar surface multiple leakage extraction performance for LPMO and FLPMO, while showing that the scaled point-by-point division in FLPMO is approximately 40 times faster on real data sets than the shaping regularization-based inversion in LPMO.</jats:p>
title: Fast local primary-and-multiple orthogonalization for surface-related multiple leakage estimation and extraction

<jats:p>Surface-related multiple elimination (SRME) has already been proven as a solid multiple and primary estimation tool for decades due to its data-driven property and strong physics behind. However, surface-related multiple leakage is still commonly seen in the SRME processed results, which might arise from the imperfect sampling and the balancing effect of the adaptive subtraction. Local primary-and-multiple orthogonalization (LPMO) is recently proposed to mitigate the multiple leakage. LPMO framework includes two separate steps: an initial multiple and primary estimation step via conservative SRME and an external multiple leakage extraction step via LPMO. Although decent leakage extraction can be achieved, LPMO requires a large computational cost due to many conjugate-gradient iterations within the shaping regularization based inversion framework. Assuming that the scalar LPMO weight is closely related to its neighboring time-and-space points, a scaled point-by-point division can be used to avoid the iterative inversion of LPMO. Therefore, we propose a fast LPMO (FLPMO) for surface-related multiple estimation. Applications on two different field data sets demonstrate the nearly same multiple leakage extraction performances for both LPMO and FLPMO, while showing that, the FLPMO is much faster than LPMO.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction has emerged as a crucial topic in the area of Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) to improve scheduled maintenance and to avoid engineering failures. This paper proposes a similarity-based methodology to perform accurate RUL prediction with model explainability and scalability. The proposed method firstly employs a Deep Similarity Learning (DSL) module with the combination of convolutional layers and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) to learn the temporal dependencies among the Run-To-Failure (R2F) profiles. Triplet loss is optimized to compress the temporal patterns into embedding spaces, which provides explainability by measuring the R2F profile distances in the embedding space. Afterwards, an ensemble regression model is applied to perform RUL prediction which empowers the proposed method with scalability and flexibility. The model performance is evaluated and benchmarked on the public aero-engine dataset and semiconductor dataset respectively. Experimental results indicate the effectiveness, flexibility and superiority of the proposed model compared with benchmarks from recent literature.</jats:p>

<jats:p>We introduce CDS-Polytope, a parameter-free framework for detecting critical transitions in 4D event clouds by discretizing the unit 3-sphere onto the 24-cell regular polytope. The 24-cell — the uniqueself-dualregularpolytopeinfourdimensions— provides24axis-labeledreference directionswithF4symmetry(order1152),enablinganintrinsicallyinterpretablesimilarity measure without training data or hyperparameter tuning. The core indicator, cosD, measures the cosine distance between the empirical vertex occupancy distribution and the uniform baseline; we demonstrate empirically that cosD is a surrogate Lyapunov exponent, tracking the order-to-chaos transition of the Lorenz system across the critical parameter rho = 24.74. A second indicator, D_eff,recoversthe fractaldimension ofthe Lorenz strange attractor(D2 = 2.06)from real Northwest Pacific typhoon track data (71,161 points, 1951-2023), yielding D_eff = 1.991 with a difference of 0.069. Three independent physical domains are validated with zero code changes between them: seismology (retroactive recovery of the Kato etal.2012 foreshock migration sequencetowithin0.52degrees),typhoonclimatology(PDO xENSO xlunarphasetriple synchrony, p = 0.000027), and ENSO dynamics (V22 to V23 vertex transition coinciding with the 1987 PDO regime shift). The framework provides explainability by construction: each of the 24 vertices carries a human-readable axis-combination label (e.g., lon+lat-dep+time-), making model decisions directly auditable. We discuss implications for explainable AI (XAI), neuromorphic computing as an edge-of-chaos feedback monitor, and digital-analog hybrid AI systems.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>We introduce CDS-Polytope, a parameter-free framework for detecting critical transitions in 4D event clouds by discretizing the unit 3-sphere onto the 24-cell regular polytope. The 24-cell — the uniqueself-dualregularpolytopeinfourdimensions— provides24axis-labeledreference directionswithF4symmetry(order1152),enablinganintrinsicallyinterpretablesimilarity measure without training data or hyperparameter tuning. The core indicator, cosD, measures the cosine distance between the empirical vertex occupancy distribution and the uniform baseline; we demonstrate empirically that cosD is a surrogate Lyapunov exponent, tracking the order-to-chaos transition of the Lorenz system across the critical parameter rho = 24.74. A second indicator, D_eff,recoversthe fractaldimension ofthe Lorenz strange attractor(D2 = 2.06)from real Northwest Pacific typhoon track data (71,161 points, 1951-2023), yielding D_eff = 1.991 with a difference of 0.069. Three independent physical domains are validated with zero code changes between them: seismology (retroactive recovery of the Kato etal.2012 foreshock migration sequencetowithin0.52degrees),typhoonclimatology(PDO xENSO xlunarphasetriple synchrony, p = 0.000027), and ENSO dynamics (V22 to V23 vertex transition coinciding with the 1987 PDO regime shift). The framework provides explainability by construction: each of the 24 vertices carries a human-readable axis-combination label (e.g., lon+lat-dep+time-), making model decisions directly auditable. We discuss implications for explainable AI (XAI), neuromorphic computing as an edge-of-chaos feedback monitor, and digital-analog hybrid AI systems.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The dynamic and unpredictable nature of seismic hazards in underground coal mines demands accurate and reliable forecasting to ensure safety in mining operations. Traditional hazard assessment approaches often fail to capture the intricate non-linear patterns underlying seismic activity and often overlook the inherent class imbalance between high and low-energy seismic events. This study aims to investigate the predictive performance of ensemble models for forecasting high-energy (E&gt;104J) seismic bumps. This study adopts some novel steps including the one-hot encoding technique for categorical feature handling, the SMOTETomek resampling technique to address class imbalance and sensitivity analysis to evaluate the contribution of individual features to hazard prediction. Four ensemble learning based boosting algorithms (AdaBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost) are implemented using a highly imbalanced micro-seismic monitoring dataset comprising 170 hazardous and 2414 non-hazardous instances. The models were evaluated through standard classification metrics including accuracy, precision, recall and F1-scores. Among the models, AdaBoost and XGBoost exhibited poor performance. Although LightGBM achieved a high precision of 96.1% but it’s relatively low recall score for hazardous states limits its effectiveness for hazard prediction. In contrast, CatBoost model exhibited reliable performance across both classes, achieving a recall score of 97.4% and predicting 166 out of 170 hazardous instances. Furthermore, sensitivity analysis using SHAP revealed that gpuls is the most significant predictor variable while features (nbumps5- nbumps89) had negligible impact to hazard prediction. Overall this data-driven study advances the forecasting of hazardous seismic events by effectively addressing class imbalnce, providing engineers valuable insights for hazard mitigation strategies and contribute to improve safety and operational resilience in underground mining environments.</jats:p>
title: Ensemble Learning-Based Seismic Hazard Forecasting for Safety Enhancement in Underground Coal Mine

items.abstract: <jats:p>Integrating the three in-situ test databases of standard penetration test, cone penetration test, and shear velocity test to build a hybrid seismic liquefaction prediction model not only helps to improve the prediction accuracy but also overcomes the problem of conflicting prediction results that are obtained by the three models based on different in-situ tests. In addition, the Bayesian network (BN) method is widely used in seismic liquefaction prediction, but there is no research on integrating different BN models for liquefaction prediction. Therefore, this study proposes to integrate these three in-situ test databases to construct different ensemble BN prediction models for seismic liquefaction using three different ensemble modes such as sequential, parallel, and hybrid. After comparing these ensemble BN models with single base BN models, the results show that the performance of the ensemble BN models is much better than the single BN models in the prediction of seismic liquefaction. The BN model with parallel mode performs the best in the ensemble models, and the sequential mode of the BN model performs the second best, whereas the hybrid mode is the worst. Generally, the base model with higher classification accuracy should rank first as it is beneficial to obtain a sequential or hybrid model with better performance. The reasons for these conclusions are subsequently discussed. In addition, comparing different random forest (RF) models that contain 100 decision trees, the parallel BN model composed of three basic BN models is comparable to the RF model.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
        <jats:p>The existing Siamese trackers have achieved increasingly successful results in visual object tracking. However, the interactive fusion among multi-layer similarity maps after cross-correlation has not been fully studied in previous Siamese network-based methods. To address this issue, we propose a novel SiamSMN for visual object tracking, which consists of feature extraction network, multi-scale fusion module and prediction head. First, the feature extraction network is used to extract the features of the template image and the search image, which is calculated by a depth-wise cross-correlation operation to produce multiple similarity feature maps. Second, we propose an effective multi-scale fusion module that can extract global context information for object search and learn the interdependencies between multi-level similarity maps. In addition, to further improve tracking accuracy, we design a learnable prediction head module to generate a boundary point for each side based on the coarse bounding box, which can solve the problem of inconsistent classification and regression during the tracking. Extensive experiments on four public benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed tracker has a competitive performance among other state-of-the-art trackers.</jats:p>
title: SiamSMN: Similarity Map Fusion Siamese Network for Visual Object Tracking

                    Previously, tokamak research has been focused mainly on large aspect ratio devices where the vessel/plasma major radius is about a factor three larger than the plasma radius. This research culminated in the design and construction of the international thermonuclear experimental reactor, ITER. Spherical tokamaks (ST), with aspect ratio below two, represent an attractive alternative to large aspect ratio tokamaks as, in our opinion, provide a faster, more economical and compact solution on the path to a fusion reactor. STs are the focus of research at Tokamak Energy Ltd with its present device ST40 in operation and the first ST reactor being designed, taking advantage of the high temperature superconductor (HTS) technology. HTS allow to design a ST with magnetic field/comparable or exceeding that of present-day large aspect ratio tokamaks. However, plasma studies carried out so far on compact, low aspect ratio tokamaks have been limited to small, low magnetic field, low plasma-current devices and therefore the data available for extrapolating to large scale ST plasmas is limited. This paper addresses the problem of scaling the results of large aspect ratio tokamak and existing ST plasmas to a high field ST reactor using plasma-similarity arguments in order to mitigate its design and operational risks. The role of the plasma aspect ratio in scaling burning plasmas as well as conventional experiments in deuterium is highlighted. We find that the scaling for fusion-reactor plasmas exhibit a stronger dependence on the magnetic field and aspect ratio than the one of conventional non-burning plasmas. <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>One of the challenging issues of using 4D seismic data into reservoir history matching is to compare the measured data to the model data in a consistent way. It is important to decide which kind of seismic data can be best used and at which level of history matching process they can be integrated. In this work, we have performed 4D seismic history matching of a sector model based on a North sea reservoir in the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) framework and have investigated the effects of different types of time-difference seismic data to update reservoir models. The reservoir-seismic model system consists of a commercial reservoir simulator coupled to an implemented rock physics model and a forward seismic modeling tool based on 1D convolution with weak contrast reflectivity approximation. The objective of this work is to investigate the sensitivity of different combinations of production and seismic data on EnKF model updating. The uncertain static reservoir parameters considered are porosity and permeability; dynamic variables such as pressure and water saturation are conditioned to both production and seismic data. In particular, we are interested to quantify the performance of the wells; also to match seismic data and to estimate the reservoir parameters. In most of the cases of reservoir characterization, time-difference impedance data performed better than time-difference amplitude data and considerably reduced posterior ensemble spread. The matching of seismic data generally improved with the inclusion of time-difference seismic data. In estimating posterior porosity and permeability, seismic difference data provided better estimate than using only production data, especially in aquifer region and also in areas that might be considered for in-fill wells. Thus, in our realistic synthetic case based on a full field reservoir model, we experienced that the integration of seismic data in the elastic domain provided better performance than using amplitude data. In addition, we investigated the effects of vertical resolution of seismic data on EnKF model updating, and showed that the choice of wavelet discretization points can have significant influence on the quality of history matching.</jats:p>
title: Ensemble Based 4D Seismic History Matching: Integration of Different Levels and Types of Seismic Data

<jats:p xml:lang="en">Denison Mine, Elliot Lake, was chosen as a site to conduct a seismic survey using a portable seismograph acquired by CANMET. During the approximate four-month period, 370 seismic events were recorded. Of that number, 342 were classified as blasts, and 28 as
mining induced seismic, MIS, events, including a 1.9 mN rockburst.
Waveform analysis was performed on these data and the results are in good agreement with those from other Northern Ontario mines.</jats:p>

items.abstract: Image retrieval predominantly relies on embedding techniques, which represent visual data as numerical vectors to enable efficient and scalable similarity comparisons. Such embeddings are crucial for a variety of computer vision tasks, including image similarity search, image classification, object detection, and facial recognition. However, conventional techniques that rely on single-network architectures or domain-specific optimizations haveing limited capability to capture the essential and complex visual information required for precise and effective similar image retrieval. To address this limitation, SET-CNN (Stacked Ensemble of CNNs), a novel framework that integrates three diverse pretrained CNN models, DenseNet121, ResNet50, and VGG16 for generating robust image embeddings and enhancing similarity retrieval is proposed. This approach extracts and stacks high-level feature vectors from each base model, concatenates them via feature-level fusion, and processes the unified representation through a meta-model optimized using triplet semi-hard loss to enhance discriminability in the embedding space. Extensive experiments on the CIFAR-10 dataset demonstrate that SET-CNN consistently outperforms individual CNNs and state-of-the-art retrieval methods, achieving a peak training MAP@5 of 0.9286 and a testing MAP@5 of 0.8745, with minimal overfitting. This represents a 7.6% improvement over the best-performing base model. Compared to Deep Semantic Ranking Hashing and Deep Supervised Hashing, SET-CNN delivers absolute gains of +8.6% and +19.9% in MAP@5, respectively, while matching the performance of more complex ResNet attention pooling models without specialized architectural modifications. Embedding quality is assessed through K-Means clustering combined with t-SNE visualization, while final similarity matching is performed using K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) with cosine similarity. These clustering and retrieval analyses confirm that the ensemble produces semantically rich and well-separated embeddings, translating into more accurate and relevant retrieval results. Given its performance and flexibility, SET-CNN offers a promising direction for developing generalizable, ensemble-based retrieval systems, with potential extensions to large-scale, multimodal datasets and real-time deployment.
title: SET-CNN: Stacked Ensemble of CNNs for Robust Image Embedding and Similarity Retrieval

items.abstract: <jats:p>The local self-similarity descriptor is a kind of important image or video local feature description method. It is often used for detection, identification and recognition. In this paper we propose a new local self-similarity descriptor based on structural similarity (SSIM) index. It is showed in this paper that the SSIM Index give very different answers to the question of how self-similar local patches really are. For a given image we compute SSIM index distances between representations for all pairs of spatial-patches and store the results in a Self-Similarity Matrix (SSM) defined as the local feature descriptor. This new method is easily extended to the wavelet representation of images. Comparative evaluation of local feature descriptor with previous methods demonstrates improved performance.</jats:p>
title: A New Local Self-Similarity Descriptor Based on Structural Similarity Index

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:p>
                  Peptide hormones are genome-encoded signal transduction molecules released in multicellular organisms. The dysregulation of hormone release can cause multiple health problems and it is crucial to study these hormones for therapeutic purposes. To help the research community working in this field, we developed a prediction server that classifies hormonal peptides and non-hormonal peptides. The dataset used in this study was collected for both plants and animals from Hmrbase2 and PeptideAtlas databases. It comprises non-redundant 1174 hormonal and 1174 non-hormonal peptide sequences which were combined and divided into 80% training and 20% validation sets. We extracted a wide variety of compositional features from these sequences to develop various Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models. The best performing model was logistic regression model trained on top 50 features which achieved an AUROC of 0.93. To enhance the performance of ML model, we applied Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) to identify hormonal sequences using similarity among them, and motif search using Motif-Emerging and Classes-Identification (MERCI) to detect motifs present in hormonal and non-hormonal sequences. We combined our best performing classification model, i.e., logistic regression model with BLAST and MERCI to form a hybrid model that can predict hormonal peptide sequences accurately. The hybrid model is able to achieve an AUROC of 0.96, an accuracy of 89.79%, and an MCC of 0.8 on the validation set.
